1.	Has the Department of National Health and Welfare carried out any study of the effects of the fluoridation of water on dental decay?
2.	If so, has the department at any time, as a result of this study or for any other reason, endorsed the fluoridation of water supplies?
3.	Has the Department of National Health and Welfare, at any time, given counsel or expressed any official opinion with respect to the fluoridation of water supplies?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (for the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The answer to part 1 of this question is that the Department of National Health and Welfare, working in co-operation with the Ontario department of health and with the local health authorities of Brant county, Lambton health unit (Sarnia), and the municipality of Stratford, has conducted a study during the past 14 years of the general effects of water fluoridation.
The answer to part 2 is that the Department of National Health and Welfare has limited its work on fluoridation to research and to official statistical reports of the findings. It has made no official recommendations for or against the adoption of this measure.
The answer to part 3 is that the department has not given any counsel or expressed any official opinion with respect to fluoridation. However, the department has made public the fact that its studies indicate that fluoridation reduces the incidence of tooth decay by about two thirds among those brought up from birth on a water supply containing about one part per million of fluoride.

At the resolution stage yesterday there were indications in all parts of the house of approval of the principle and purpose of this measure as well as of the procedure that was suggested, and in view of that fact I think it may be assumed that the bill does meet with the approval of the house and that the house has welcomed the suggestion that immediately following second reading of the measure it should be referred to the banking and commerce committee. speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ARTICLES OF AGREEMENT AND PAYMENT OF SUBSCRIPTION

Support by this party of the principle embodied in this bill has already been indicated. It is not my intention to take up any time this morning. Therefore its aims appeal to us all.
We' approve the principle of the bill, and we approve the procedures which have been outlined by the minister as to dealing with the bill in committee.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ARTICLES OF AGREEMENT AND PAYMENT OF SUBSCRIPTION
speechtext:
also wish to support the proposition now before us, and I also want to compliment the government on submitting this proposal by way of legislation to the House of Commons.
As the minister knows, Canada also became a member of another international corporation-the International Finance Corporation, I believe, was its name-which is also affiliated with the international bank. That was only done by way of a vote in the estimates. speechtext:
Resolved,-That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act to provide:
1.	That the sales tax on electric heating equipment, designed for use on a system using 230 volts or greater, for permanent installation as part of an electric heating system for buildings, be repealed, but not including electric wiring or other materials leading to or connecting such equipment to the electric power supply.
Excise Tax Act
2.	That ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings, but not including materials used in their manufacture, be exempt from sales tax.
3.	That the sales tax on laryngeal speaking aids and parts therefor, including batteries specifically designed for use therewith, be repealed.
4.	That the sales tax on prepared surgical sutures be repealed.
5.	That the sales tax on goods enumerated in customs tariff item 692a, that is, "articles presented from abroad in recognition of the saving of human life", be repealed.
6.	That the sales tax on perlite be repealed.
7.	That portrait photographs of individuals be exempt from sales tax.
8.	That the exemption from sales tax for,
"perforated bituminized fibre pipe for drainage
purposes not exceeding four inches in inside diameter"
be changed to read,
"perforated pipe for drainage purposes not exceeding four inches in inside diameter".
9.	That the exemption from sales tax for feeds and feed supplements be extended to include feed supplements for addition to feeds for fur-bearing animals, and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture thereof.
10.	That hardware for doors and sash not specifically mentioned in schedule III be excluded from the sales tax exemption for articles and materials to be used in the manufacture of building materials.
11.	That the exemption from sales tax for,
"septic tanks"
be changed to read,
"septic tanks and grease traps therefor".
12.	That the exemption from sales tax for,
"Usual coverings to be used exclusively for
covering goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture of such coverings" be changed to read,
"Usual coverings or containers to be used exclusively for covering or containing goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax and to be delivered and sold with the goods, and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture of such coverings or containers".
13.	That the exemption from sales tax for. Materials for use only in the construction,
equipment and repair of ships over ten tons net register tonnage" be changed to read,
Materials for use only in the equipment and repair of ships over ten tons net register tonnage".
14.	That the security required under the Excise Tax Act include bonds or other securities of or guaranteed by the government of Canada.
15.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of April, I960.
On paragraph 2.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are on paragraph 2. Yesterday the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam offered an amendment to this paragraph as follows:
That the resolution be amended by eliminating therefrom the words "but not including materials used in their manufacture."
I understand that the hon. member for Carleton wanted to raise a point of order on this amendment.

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it was my intention when the amendment was moved to raise a point of order, but my researches have indicated to me that it would not be judicious to do so.
I wish the Minister of Finance would follow that course.

I wish to offer a few words of explanation. Under existing conditions a manufacturer is able to retail to a user a warm air heating system, and if he does so he has to collect an 11 per cent tax only on the materials used in the manufacture; but if the manufacturer disposes of the article to a wholesaler he is obligated to make the wholesaler pay an 11 per cent tax on the whole article. The wholesaler is therefore placed at a considerable disadvantage. Since labour is a large component of the cost of these heating units I feel this is not right and does not reflect the intention of the government. The object of the amendment is to place the wholesalers on the same level as the manufacturer in so far as the amount of sales tax is concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
situation in respect of this is that the exclusion from the exemption of materials used in the manufacture of ducts for heating systems conforms with what has been the previous tax situation. When these products of the tinsmith's trade were free from tax because the tinsmith was classed as a small manufacturer, the raw materials he purchased were not exempt. Moreover, these ducts might be manufactured in shops that produce taxable products as well as tax exempt heating ducts. In such cases it would be extremely difficult from an administrative point of view to keep account of and to restrict the tax exemption to the sheet metals going into heating ducts. I think in that situation the hon. gentleman will probably realize that what he seeks to do by the amendment is to create a situation which administratively would not be feasible.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 19; nays, 83.

The situation dealt with by this paragraph creates a problem for the average small home owner as a result of the new regulations introduced. I have had occasion to refer to this previously. Notwithstanding the remarks of the Minister of Finance with respect to the regulations concerning tinsmiths, we can see today that the position of the tinsmith is definitely not the same as it was a year ago. We have heard about government by order in council, and so on, but in this instance we have had government 'by interpretation.
I The Chairman.]
I am informed that the tinsmiths in Canada were first advised that the regulations would take effect in July of 1959. If that is not correct the minister is free to say so. At that time instructions were given to the effect that the tinsmiths would come under sales tax on the products they manufacture and sell, and would lose the exemption previously accorded them under the regulations. I realize that section 34 of the Excise Tax Act gives the minister power to issue instructions that would cancel the previous instructions. For some reason not explained the people affected by those instructions were later informed that the regulations would not come into effect until January 1, 1960. Hon. members began to receive protests from the people concerned. If my information is correct the minister later apparently postponed the effective date from January 1 to July 1, 1960. That is how it stands today.
Last evening the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance read a paragraph from a letter which appeared to congratulate the minister on what he was doing, but in my opinion the tinsmiths of this country are not in the position they were in previously.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister some of the items which necessarily, under these new regulations, will be taxed henceforth. This will result in adding to the cost of home construction. Once again this government will be responsible for striking at the Canadian small home owner who will have to pay additional taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is utter
balderdash.

I can tell the minister who now objects that in this respect the home owner will henceforth be taxed, which was not the case previously. I understand that on the conventional home this will run as high as $250, and if the material used is copper it will run to $900 or $1,000. These are estimates that I have received from people who know what they are talking about.
Oh, oh.

The material is taxable. The difference between the cost of eavestroughing is such that if copper is used it will cost you definitely at least four times as much.
We were informed a moment ago by the parliamentary secretary that he did not wish to accept the amendment presented by the hon. member because it would cause confusion in administration. May I remind the parliamentary secretary and the minister that under a clause which we shall be discussing in a moment, namely clause No. 12, coverings

or containers are exempt. If the material used by tinsmiths was also exempt from excise tax, in what way would that be confusing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the hon. member is discussing an amendment which has just been disposed of by the committee.

I am not discussing the amendment, nor do I wish to bring it back. Since this paragraph has not been passed as yet, I am just making reference to the argument that the material, which is the matter under discussion, be not exempt from sales tax. The paragraph reads:
That ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings, but not including materials used in their manufacture, be exempt from sales tax.
The opinion of the minister, as explained by his parliamentary secretary, is that the tinsmiths of this country should be taxed because it would be confusing to the administration if they were not. In a few moments we will consider another paragraph which should receive some attention. Since the materials used in the fabrication of the articles under that clause are exempt from sales tax, the articles themselves should be exempt. Surely there cannot be two arguments about the difficulty of administration and the confusion which may be created. Air conditioning units which may be installed in a building are not exempt. This is further taxation.
We realize that today our workers, and especially the workers in my area, require the very best of conditions in their homes. We know that in 1960 this type of unit or installation is commonly used, much more so than 15 or 20 years ago. We are trying to prevent the betterment of our worker by putting a tax on those things. Ventilation in our homes today is not a luxury. We have dryers in homes and the people should have them. The worker will have to pay a special tax on any special installation he may require for the ventilation of dryers. Today kitchens have ventilation systems, and they should have them. Tinsmiths will be taxed on installations in kitchens, which was not the case before.
We do this when people are anxious to have a better standard of living. People should be able to afford and can afford to have better facilities and modern homes, yet we are bringing in a clause in 1960 which taxes them and puts an added cost on the homes of those workers who should have those facilities.
Under this paragraph the material is taxed. I do feel that the government should pay attention to the representations which were
Excise Tax Act
made to the minister. Undoubtedly his actions indicate that the people of Canada have made numerous representations to him. A few months ago I had occasion to make reference to representations made by some people in my area. Representations were made by the tinsmiths' association through Mr. McCoy. I do not wish to read the letter to the Minister of Finance, but I must say that he was wrong when he indicated to me in the house that the regulations we were discussing at that time had been done away with and that the tinsmiths were not in a position different from that which they enjoyed before.
Notwithstanding the congratulations which the parliamentary secretary read last night, it is not quite the true story of the position of the tinsmiths in Canada, especially as it affects the consumers. I am thinking of the consumers because hon. members should realize that the 11 per cent tax which is levied is not paid in the long run by the manufacturers or the tinsmiths. They pass it on. It will be simply added to the cost of the installation which the tinsmith is making, and it will be passed on to the user or the contractor. The man who will pay it in the end is the worker or the person for whom the building is being constructed or the unit installed.
I feel the minister should think over his proposition which he mentioned some months ago, the effect of which has been postponed. We should return to the condition that existed before this amendment was introduced, so that the maximum number of houses would be built. We have few houses being built in our country today owing to the money situation. If the minister accepted my suggestions at least the houses which are built would be built at a minimum cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member has evidently quite misapprehended the effect of the present proposal. I would hate, in the light of what he has said today, to entrust him with any estimates of the cost of house construction or any attribute of it. This, Mr. Chairman, is a relieving provision. If the hon. member does not want to introduce this form of taxation relief, then of course his proper course is to oppose the resolution. This is a relieving provision; I wish to make that clear.
In the second place, it would have the effect of removing the existing discrimination. I do not think hon. members wish to see discriminations existing in this field. When tinsmiths were originally exempted as a class under the regulations to which he has referred-and in this respect it is not the Minister of Finance but the Minister of National Revenue under whose authority those

Excise Tax Act
regulations are made, the authority being given by act of parliament-there was a large number of smaller operators doing their own work with hand tools. With the change in economic conditions and techniques, tinsmith-ing operations have changed into a full-fledged business, each manufacturing an extensive variety of goods made out of all kinds of sheet metal, including among other things such major items as lockers, tanks, cabinets, shelving and so forth. In other words, it has developed that operators who were claiming to be exempt as tinsmiths were in fact manufacturers of metal products and were competing on a tax-free basis with other manufacturers of metal products who had to pay sales tax on what they produced.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite clear that this provision will have the effect of relieving the situation and removing a patent discrimination, where some persons have been taking advantage of a provision which was never intended by parliament to be used in the way in which they have been using it.

I should like to say a few words on this subject, because I have been a tinsmith all my life. This is not a new subject; this idea of paying sales tax on manufactured goods worth over $3,000 has been in force for years, but it was never enforced on small tinsmiths.
It is a good move that warm air ducts are not to be subject to sales tax, because most of the shops throughout the country which are installing furnaces and air conditioning units are small shops. They buy all their fittings in manufactured form, and the sales tax has already been paid on those fittings. Sales tax has always been paid on furnaces and fittings and so on before they come to the shop after being purchased from the large manufacturers. Therefore the exemption from sales tax of ducts for warm air heating systems and for air conditioning is a move in the right direction, because it means the doing away with the payment of an unnecessary tax by the tinsmiths who make the installations.
I suggest that the small shops that employ only one or two men should be exempt from the sales tax requirement, because they are not in the manufacturing class. That is where the big trouble arises. The small operator who has only one, two or three men working for him is practically working for the government now, because he has to make unemployment insurance and income tax payments, and so on. If he has to make sales tax payments too it will mean he will have to hire somebody to look after these things. We have always paid sales tax on such items as

eavestroughs, conductor pipes and so on that we have bought. The proposal to remove the sales tax from warm air ducts is a good move because it helps the householder.
One hon. member said that it would increase the cost of an installation in a home by $200. I should like to go to that district where they are getting that kind of money, because in our section of the country we certainly do not get that kind of money and could not increase the price by $200 for a home installation. The difference in the price of materials about which he spoke certainly does not amount to $200 to $800 in a home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
following what has been said by the hon. member for Brantford, I think the committee will recall what was said last night by my parliamentary secretary in emphasizing that the proposed change in the regulations concerning tinsmiths will not change the present practice of not imposing a sales tax on sheet metal work done on a construction site, such as installing flashings or doing roof work.

Mr. Chairman, I am looking at the wording of the section. Does the minister not think the wording could be much more explanatory of what it is intended to achieve? When we look at it now we see that ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings, but not the materials, are to be exempt. Ducts consist of two things, the material and the labour that goes into making the ducts. Would it not be much simpler and clearer if we said that the labour that goes into these things shall be exempt from sales tax? Inasmuch as a duct is the material and the empty space, if we say that the material shall not be exempt then we are only exempting the empty space, the piping, the air space. I think the provision should be clarified, because as I read it now ducts for warm air systems shall be exempt but not the materials. What then is exempt? Is it the labour or is it the air space?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is being
exempted is everything that goes into the sale price. The suggestion of the hon. member would involve a revolutionary change in the whole basis of the Excise Tax Act, because the principle of that act is to levy a percentage tax on the sale price when sold at the manufacturer's or producer's level. It would not be possible to take that price and break it down into component parts. I do not know how you would isolate certain elements that enter into the sale price. It would be a hopeless undertaking. In any event, I must point out to the hon. member that his suggestion is completely hostile to the present principle and basis of the whole act.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support very briefly the approach to this problem expressed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Nickel Belt, because I am of the opinion that the government's policy should be to do everything possible to reduce the cost of housing. Housing is a very important matter to working people particularly, and my criticism of this arrangement is simply that under present circumstances I think the government should do everything it can with respect to taxation and within the limits of its other powers to lower the cost of housing as much as possible. This is a serious matter to working people generally. I think the hon. member for Nickel Belt was a bit out of line when he suggested two or three hundred dollars, but even if there is an extra cost of $20 to $50 on the average house-
I did not say that.

Pardon me; I understood the hon. member to say that the extra cost would be about $200. I may have misunderstood him. But even if it is only $20 to $50 it is an additional cost, and I think that in line with the needs of today the government should consider doing what it can to assist in this direction. On that account I should like the minister to inform the committee the reason for the decision to tax the materials that go into heating ducts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With respect, I must say that I think the hon. member has misapprehended the effect of the resolution. The resolution is a relieving provision. Its purpose is to create an exemption in respect of ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings where an exemption did not exist before. Far from increasing the cost of construction to small or large home owners, the effect of this provision is more likely to be to reduce the cost because, you see, the exemption that he speaks of applied previously only in the case of purchases from a particular source, and now the exemption will apply in the home owner's favour wherever he acquires his ducts for warm air heating.
I think there has been a total misapprehension in the discussion and the remarks of some hon. members opposite as to the effect of the resolution. This is more likely to reduce the cost of home construction to the small home owner than to increase it, and at the same time we are removing a discrimination.

I quite understand that this is a partial benefit, but in view of the housing situation I wanted to know the reason for
Excise Tax Act
the government's decision not to remove the excise tax completely from this heating equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member talked about this heating equipment, but the equipment we are discussing consists of ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings. That is what is to be exempted here. To go on and say that we should extend the exemption as well to the materials used in their manufacture would be taking us into some very doubtful realms. I have given, and my parliamentary secretary gave last night, very sound reasons for this resolution being in its present form. I can repeat those reasons, but I do submit in all earnestness to the hon. member, whose concern in these matters is recognized by all members of the committee, that to interpret this resolution as one likely to increase the cost of home construction is quite wrong.
The hon. member for Brantford, who has had more firsthand experience with this business than any other member of the house and who has studied it very carefully, has given most convincing reasons for support of the resolution in its present form.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose I should be entitled not to present a rebuttal but to explain what I said before. I said that for an average size home it would cost roughly $275 or $300 to have the job done if tin were used, and if copper were used the cost would be between $900 and $1,000. That is the cost I have obtained, and the hon. member for Brantford should agree that this is roughly correct. We were told by the minister that was the amount on which the buyer of this material would have to pay tax, and on $300 that would be $33 or more which he would have to pay. If the man chose copper as the material he would have to pay roughly $110 extra. My neighbour happened to have this job done last week, and over the week end I asked him what it did cost. He gave me the price.
Surely there must be an average price. I realize that the size of the home and possibly the type of roof construction would make some difference to the cost of a watershed built around the roof. Surely the minister agrees that the amounts given by me are proper. I do not say that would be the whole amount, but it would be terrible if the government were to add $33 to the cost of a house because when you consider the amount these people borrow and repay over 25 years it might mean the addition of $75 to the cost of a house.
I am surprised that the minister did not answer some of my questions. The minister

Excise Tax Act
mentioned that this is a relieving section, but it has been a relieving section only since May 6.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I realize why the minister may be getting to his feet. I realize there was no amendment of May 6 to this paragraph. The amendment of May 6 refers to paragraph 12 which we will be discussing later and about which the minister certainly made a volte face in relation to the position he had previously taken. This second exemption is partial. There are taxes which will have to be paid by the people who contract to have homes built. These taxes will be an added expense. The hon. member for Brantford has not told me what the added taxes will be if the home owner wants to have a special installation extending 20 to 25 feet to properly ventilate a dryer, or 20 to 25 feet in order to properly ventilate a kitchen. I have not been told what the additional cost to the home builder would be in relation to air conditioning.
I do believe the people interested in these items were slightly pleased when they were instructed recently that some relief would be given to them, especially when one considers the notification they received earlier that they would now become taxable and would not be considered as small manufacturers. I must congratulate the government for at least bringing in a partial exemption. However, the government has not introduced an exemption which would put the small home builder in the position in which he was under the previous administration.
This is the answer I should like to obtain from the minister. This is a relieving section to some extent. We have taken away 100 per cent and we are giving somebody back 20 per cent, and we call that a relieving section. This is the explanation I should like to obtain from the minister. It is the consumer of the services offered by the tinsmith, the home builder, the worker, who is suffering, not the tinsmith. If a person ordered copper flashing which the tinsmith agreed to install for $900, the tinsmith would have to pay roughly $110 in tax. I do not believe the tinsmith would take that loss, so the flashing would cost the man about $1,110. I am speaking on behalf of those people who use the services of the tinsmith, not necessarily the tinsmith. I believe it is a known fact in this country that people measure the amount of profit they can make, and if a tax is placed on their work, then that tax is passed along to the consumer.

I should like to make a few remarks on the subject to which the hon. member for Nickel Belt
has referred. It is obvious that he knows nothing about the heating business. If a warm air heating unit is installed in a home today the average cost on a project basis is between $525 and $650. This is for the furnace, the burner, the oil tank and the duct system. The duct work, which is the thing we are discussing today, will cost between $125 and $200, and it is being exempted from tax at the present time.
The hon. member talks about a copper installation in connection with warm air heating units and air conditioning. I have yet to find such a copper installation in my part of the country.

Would the hon. member permit me to say that I was discussing drainage systems and roof flashings, which are not exempt under this section. I was not talking about the things which are exempt. I am talking about ventilation, which is not exempt, and air conditioning, which is not exempt, as well as the drainage for roofs, which is not exempt.

In so far
as air conditioning is concerned, when the furnace is installed in the basement of a house and the piping is made up, they use the same pipes for the air conditioning that they use for the warm air heating. They do not run a separate pipe system, and this duct work is exempt for the warm air heating system because that is what it is used for in the wintertime. The hon. member says that this government is increasing the cost, which is not true.

In reply to the hon. member for Nickel Belt may I say that it is stated right in the bill that flashings are exempt. It does not matter whether you in-stal copper flashings or galvanized iron flashings, they are exempt from this sales tax. In so far as the warm air ducts are concerned, we have always paid sales tax on the material as it comes to our shops. The tinsmith pays sales tax on the materials. However, under this new regulation we do not pay sales tax on the cost of manufacturing the warm air ducts as we were required to do before. It is at this point that the saving comes in.
In so far as the cost of installation is concerned, we do a lot of installations in my home town and the average price for installing an air conditioning unit is running between $250 and $275, that is for piping the unit. When this new regulation becomes effective there will be no sales tax paid on the ducts we make up to go into the unit, and this would result is a saving to the home builder when he is having the unit installed.

In so far as eavestroughing is concerned, the average price of eavestroughing for the homes that are being built in Brantford or anywhere in southern Ontario is running between $75 and $100, that is for labour and everything. It does not cost $275, as my hon. friend states. If one receives that amount of money for installing eavestroughing on a house in Sudbury I am going to move my shop up there tomorrow. The eavestroughing comes in already made up. I do not believe there is one manufacturer in Ontario who will make up eavestroughing by hand, because it does not pay. We can buy the eavestroughing in 10-foot lengths, already stamped out, so we do not manufacture it. We buy it from the manufacturer who pays the sales tax that the government imposes. The cost certainly does not run anywhere near $275 a house. I have been in this business since 1923, and I have yet to instal eavestroughing on a house that cost $275.

I think the hon. member for Brantford has been very helpful in explaining the present situation in connection with a trade with which he is so familiar. However, would he not agree with me that notwithstanding the exemption provided here with respect to ducts, a mistake was made when the small tinsmith was removed from the type of manufacturer listed in form ET 1 to which I referred last night, and that if he were restored to his former position it would be helpful to the small tinsmith?

The whole problem has been in trying to differentiate between a tinsmith in a small shop such as that which we operate at home, with my two sons and a couple of helpers, and a tinsmith in a large shop. Certainly if the sales tax were taken off everything we put into the home it would help us. How are we going to make a distinction between a small shop and a big one? If someone wants us to manufacture a hundred articles, we are going to do it. We therefore get into manufacturing. These shops which have 10 to 15 men and have to pay a manufacturer's licence are going to object to our doing that. It is only reasonable. But the small man who is working by himself, something which I did years ago, is not affected. It did not affect me because I never paid sales tax to the government at all on manufactured goods, because they were all brought in.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 3.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall paragraph 3 carry?

On paragraph 3 I have a few comments to make, and any remarks 1
Excise Tax Act
make on paragraph 3 would be equally appropriate to paragraph 4. The minister well knows that when he and many of his present supporters were sitting on this side of the house they felt that our list of exemptions with respect to pharmaceuticals and medical items, particularly drugs, was altogether inadequate. We know that new drugs are coming on the market and that they are extremely expensive. We are reading these days that drugs in Canada are perhaps more expensive than they are in any other part of the world.
I just want to make the point to the minister that in another year we would hope his revenues might be in a better situation and that he might find it possible to extend the list of exemptions particularly with respect to drugs. We now exempt some of the expensive drugs that came on the market a few years ago, but the list has not been added to greatly. I think that now a number of expensive drugs have been substituted. I believe a revision in this field would be fruitful to the minister prior to another budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member is referring rather to the list of drugs that may be included in the definition of medical expenses-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and which are permitted to be deducted from income in the determination of income for income tax purposes.
No. I am referring to your schedule here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was the burden of our representations in former years in opposition, and we have had an opportunity in the past two years to extend greatly the provisions of the Income Tax Act in that regard. As to exemption from sales tax-

May I correct the minister? I was not referring to that matter. I was referring to page 27 of the consolidation of the Excise Tax Act which sets out certain charitable, health and other items that are exempt from tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but the hon. gentleman purported to refer to certain principles which I have advocated in this house. That is where I think he is confusing what has been said in this respect.
As to the removal of sales tax on articles in use by persons who suffer from either an illness, necessity for surgical operation or the need of some aid such as the special aid referred to in paragraph 3 of the resolution, I think we have shown by the terms of this resolution, as on other occasions, a desire

Excise Tax Act
to make tax policy conform as far as possible to the needs of persons who suffer these misfortunes.

Arising out of what the minister has just said, which indicates the general attitude of the government toward this kind of aid, may I say this. A speaking aid naturally brings to mind a hearing aid. In fact certain kinds of hearing aids are exempt. I just wonder what the position is in a case where a hearing aid is combined with eyeglasses, as are most of the modern ones. Are they exempt when in combination as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that this nice point raised by the hon. member has not arisen for decision. A hearing aid is exempt at the present time. Eyeglasses in certain forms are not exempt. On this question of a combination, and here I am not attempting to give any interpretation that the hon. member should construe as being binding on the Department of National Revenue because the point has not arisen, I should think if the problem were presented under the law as it stands today the department would have to look at the portion of the aid which is exempt and treat it as exempt and look at that portion which is taxable and treat it as taxable. However, the point has not arisen for determination. I am simply indicating an immediate reaction to the nice question raised by the hon. member.
I can appreciate the difficulty. That is why I brought the matter to the minister's attention. Will he have his officers give some consideration to the exemption of this combination of aids?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will certainly give study to the whole question. I emphasize, however, that I am not attempting to give any interpretation for the Department of National Revenue if the question should be presented in court for decision.
One of the best known hearing aids of that type, which is a combination type, I was pricing myself, not for my own purposes fortunately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is not suffering from the infirmities of old age, is he?

I think it is the experience of most people that the price of that particular article runs to perhaps a couple of hundred dollars, and that the value of the lenses would perhaps be the price of ordinary spectacles, say $10. Therefore the proportion that is attributable to the hearing aid is the important element by far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is quite clear
that the hearing aid is exempt. Therefore I think hon. members can be reassured that the proportion in the combination attributable to the hearing aid will certainly be recognized as exempt. They need have no fear on that score.

Having regard to the comments made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in connection with pharmaceuticals and the answer given by the minister, I should like to inquire whether pharmaceuticals are now exempt or whether they are taxed, and if so to what extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are taxable now, except in the specific exemptions enumerated in the schedule, namely schedule 3 of the Excise Tax Act.
There are four.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is there a list including a number of pharmaceuticals which are exempt, but they must be mentioned specifically in order to be exempt.

As I indicated-the minister has not said so-the list is rather slender and consists of ACTH, cortisone, insulin, radium and liver extract if used in the treatment of anemia. That is the entire list. That is why I was indicating its number.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And vaccine for polio.
Yes, vaccine for poliomyelitis.

I tried to jot them down quickly. It seems to me there are six-if I was quick enough-which are now exempt. It would seem to me that the prices of drugs are high enough in Canada; in fact the indications are that they are higher in Canada than anywhere else in the world. It would seem to me that they are high enough without adding or having added or included a sales tax in the price thereof. This would appear to me to be one field which the government and the minister could explore thoroughly from the point of view of complete exemption of pharmaceuticals developed by the ethical drug industry.
I am not referring to the so-called proprietary medicines or cough syrups or things of that nature, although this is an industry which could be given some consideration also. I am referring especially to the wide range of broad spectrum antibiotics, for example tetracycline, tranquilizers and other drugs which have recently come on the market and to whose number additions are being made by the companies from time to time. As I said, it seems to me that with

Canada having to pay the highest price for its pharmaceuticals that is paid anywhere in the world, including the United States, some action might well be taken here by exempting these particular products from tax, hoping that the reduction would be passed on to the consumer for whom these drugs are prescribed.
The common price range of one capsule, for instance, in the tetracycline field is approximately 60 cents, and this is a heavy burden for an individual patient who has one of these antibiotics prescribed for him. He does not buy these drugs in lots of one, either; the normal prescription runs to 16 or thereabouts, for which the patient has to pay $8 or $9, maybe even more. We surely should not add to that burden by exacting sales tax from a consumer who finds himself in this difficult position. Inasmuch as we now exempt liver extract, ACTH, and poliomyelitis vaccine-these were the ones I was able to take down from the list that was read by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River- we should certainly extend this list to include the other types of pharmaceuticals developed by the ethical drug industry in order that we may relieve to an even greater extent the heavy burden placed on patients.
I do not know what this proposal would mean in terms of lost or decreased revenue to the government. Knowing that the drug industry is a two or three billion dollar a year industry, that is in the United States and Canada together, I realize that it could have some appreciable effect on crown revenues at a time when I know the minister is concerned seriously about the revenue and expenditure picture. However, here is a field in which immediate action is needed to relieve this onerous burden on people who through no fault of their own become ill and have to have these drugs prescribed for them. Perhaps the minister could indicate whether there has been a study made in this regard and, if so, what is the estimated revenue that accrues to the crown through sales tax on these pharmaceuticals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These matters are always under consideration. It is not possible to give a precise estimate. The cost would in any event extend into millions of dollars. How many millions, I would not be prepared to indicate at the moment. However, may I suggest we are not dealing with drugs in this item at all. We are dealing with the matter of a hearing aid. Now that the subject has been reviewed, perhaps the hon. member would be satisfied that he has put his views on the record.

We are not dealing with a hearing aid.
Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A speaking aid.

I realize that I was probably wandering further than the resolution would allow, and I appreciate the courtesy of the minister in not following his usual practice of rising on a point of order. I also appreciate your courtesy, Mr. Chairman, in allowing me to continue.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 4.

With respect to paragraph 4, I was wondering what the position is with respect to the purchase of similar articles-pharmaceuticals and other things- that go into hospitals. Has there been an exemption with respect to purchases by hospitals other than those which are operated by a provincial government? I would imagine that such hospitals would get the prescribed exemption. Would a hospital which was not owned by a federal or provincial government be able to purchase drugs and surgical sutures without tax being imposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The language of the act now exempts such articles and materials for the sole use of any bona fide public hospital certified to be such by the Department of National Health and Welfare when used exclusively by the said hospital and not for resale, and purchased in good faith.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 5.
This is an odd item. Would the minister just indicate the frequency of this event happening and what is involved. Is it a big prize?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This paragraph refers to articles presented from abroad in recognition of the saving of human life. It does not apply to the saving of political life. This paragraph is put forward with a view to exempting special awards made from abroad to persons in Canada. Tariff item 692(a) is duty free but is not listed as tax free under the Excise Tax Act. This is something which appeared in the course of a study, and I think it is obviously the sort of thing the committee would wish to bring into line.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
Paragraph 6 agreed to.
On paragraph 7.

Paragraph 7 reads:
That portrait photographs of individuals be exempt from sales tax.
I just rise to seek information from the minister. Obviously, in recognition of the

Excise Tax Act
great contribution made by this group throughout the years to the public life of Canada, some of its members have been approached by very prominent artists who wish to paint their portraits in oils in order to make sure there is no gap in the continuity-in the pictorial record-of the public figures of this nation. I am just asking the minister whether that type of portrait in oils is exempt from taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the value is more than $20, the portrait is exempt. I can well imagine that any portrait which preserves for posterity the good features of the hon. gentleman or his colleagues will certainly be a very valuable picture indeed, and consequently will be exempt.

I have previously indicated at another stage of the debate an interest in this item. I did not explain it at the time, but it arose from some inquiries I have made since January of this year with respect to an intention that was announced by the Department of National Revenue last summer to bring under tax in the future the photo finishing type of production from our photographic shops. We are back to that ET 1 form we have been discussing. Portrait photographers were listed as small manufacturers who would not have to take out the sales tax. I believe they have always escaped taxation on their production. We have, I believe, traditionally taxed what is recognized as ordinary commercial photography, but we have never imposed a tax on the cost of developing the ordinary roll of film for the general public. The department last summer indicated that they felt this should bear tax having regard to the language of the Excise Tax Act. I take it they were looking upon these people as in the nature of manufacturers or producers, and unless in some way exempted they proposed to impose a tax on this production for the first time. I believe it was to commence January 1, 1960.
Subsequently a row was raised and the department decided they were not too sure of their legal position. I am informed that a few months ago they submitted the problem to the Department of Justice. I imagine that by now the department has obtained a ruling from the Department of Justice as to whether they were right or wrong in the action they proposed to take last summer.
Would the minister give us more information concerning what has taken place? Would he confirm that my impression is right so far, and indicate what took place last summer along these lines? Would he also state what his intentions are for the future? The minister gave me a categorical answer on

April 4, that these changes in the law would in no way bring about taxation on what is known as ordinary photo finishing for the public at large.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
during studies made within the last year the Department of National Revenue inquired into the operations of photo finishers, and as a result came to the conclusion that these operations constituted manufacturing under the Excise Tax Act in the strict sense of the word. The department accordingly notified photo finishers that as of a named date they would be required to apply for manufacturers' licences under the act. There followed immediately a series of representations to the department which prompted further technical discussions between the department and the industry.
Meanwhile the Minister of National Revenue suspended the effective date of the department's notice to permit this further investigation to be carried on. Although there are some areas of production in photo finishing concerning which there is little doubt, there are others which might well be debatable, and this is recognized. There is considerable variety in the processes and noticeable differences in the final products. Accordingly it was decided that no action would be taken to require the licensing of photo finishers and the taxation of their products without specific legislation for the purpose, and no such specific legislation is being put forward.
Because of the plural reference may I ask if this is to apply only to portraits of one individual or of groups?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the word "individual" appears in the plural in this item. It has reference to as many individuals as may be discernible in any photograph.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 8.
I wonder if the minister would explain the reason for the change and indicate whether there is any discrimination between this type of material and other drainage pipe.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this paragraph of the resolution merely proposes that the words "bituminized fibre" be deleted from the sales tax exemption for perforated drainage pipe not exceeding 4 inches in inside diameter. This kind of drainage pipe is used in some cases in lieu of clay drainage tile. I understand that when the exemption was placed in the act a few years ago the only perforated tile of this dimension was made

from bituminized fibre. It has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance that this type of drainage pipe is now being manufactured out of other substances, and consequently the words "bituminized fibre" are being deleted. I am not aware of any discrimination which results.

I assume from what the parliamentary secretary has said that this applies to a type of tile ordinarily referred to as weeping tile or foundation tile, and that this is a substitute. Is that what the hon. gentleman meant?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, if it is perforated.
Does this include drainage tile for agricultural purposes? If so, why is the diameter limited to 4 inches? Occasionally it is necessary to use 6 or 8 inch pipe.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find that covered in another paragraph which refers to drainage tiles for agricultural purposes. That does not have a limitation on the basis of measurement.

Perhaps this would be a good opportunity to ask the parliamentary secretary whether it would not be advisable at this time to remove the tax from all drainage tile. As the hon. gentleman is no doubt aware, there is a rank case of discrimination in respect to sewer pipes and drainage pipes. I am sure the hon. gentleman will be particularly sympathetic today because earlier this morning his minister said-if I paraphrase him correctly-"I do not think hon. members of this committee would wish to see discrimination existing in the field of excise tax." There is a provision which permits municipalities installing sewer pipe and tile to obtain a rebate, but this unfortunately does not extend to the pipe in other municipalities which require the installation to be done by private individuals and private entrepreneurs. Consequently you have a case of discrimination, because in some municipalities the taxpayers receive the benefit of this abatement while in others operating under a different system the home owners are charged for the tax in the price of their homes.
This is a development that has taken place within the last few years. Previously the municipalities installed all local services under municipal improvement acts of one kind or another, but now they often require the subdividers to install for them sewer tiles which will be used perhaps not only locally by the houses within one area but also in a wider area. You have a dual system. You have a system where pipe installed by municipalities directly is subject to an abatement of the tax, while that
Excise Tax Act
installed by private entrepreneurs as agents for the -municipality is still subject to the tax.
Would the parliamentary secretary indicate whether the government will permit an enlargement of the tax abatement in this field in order to remove the obvious discrimination which exists at the present time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is going a considerable distance afield from this resolution, which covers only pipe not exceeding 4 inches in inside diameter. I am familiar with the situation to which the hon. gentleman refers. He will appreciate that the exemption which was introduced by this government was introduced for the purpose of providing relief for the municipalities. It was not intended as a relief to private individuals. In the operation and administration within a municipality there may be techniques adopted which do not permit the sales tax exemption to be made available, but the whole purpose has been to make the relief available to municipalities. I think that is about as far as I wish to go at the present time.

Obviously the parliamentary secretary appreciates the distinction. The same people, the same municipal taxpayers, in one municipality pay tax on the pipe which services their houses and in the neighbouring municipality they do not. This is rank discrimination. In view of what the minister said earlier I think it should be removed.
Whether it should be discussed on this item I would not wish to say categorically, Mr. Chairman, but may I just refer the parliamentary secretary to paragraph 11, where another element of discrimination is introduced. Here septic tanks installed by individuals are not subject to tax, yet where the individual is required by municipal law or regulation to instal a sewage disposal system to accomplish the same purpose he is subject to the tax. There is an obvious case of discrimination and I should like the parliamentary secretary to indicate to the committee whether he would be willing to recommend to his government that they take under immediate consideration, even before this schedule is passed, enlargement of the provision for relief of tax in respect of sewer and drainage tiles.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will realize, of course, that it lies entirely within the power of the municipality to see that the exemption which is provided by the act is in fact effective. This is a matter for administration at the municipal level, and need create no difficulty.

Excise Tax Act
I am aware that many municipalities across the country-indeed the great majority of municipalities

are carrying on subdivisions in such a way that the exemption which is intended for municipalities in fact is fully applicable, and I actually see no difficulty in any municipality so conducting its affairs that the exemption will be in fact applicable. The situation I think is really one of municipal administration rather than legislation by this parliament.

Partially, Mr. Chairman, but the problem itself is much deeper than that. The problem was created by a fundamental disparity in the division of responsibility and tax revenue among the three levels of government. If it was not for this fundamental problem undoubtedly the municipalities would not have embarked upon what is essentially a method of expediency in the financing of municipal improvements. It was never intended that municipal improvements should be unloaded on individual house builders and purchasers, but that they should be borne by the taxpayers at large. The new system has been forced on them by this lack of solution of the broader problem.
Since we are dealing specifically with the injustice to one group as against another, I wonder if the parliamentary secretary can advise the committee whether mechanics have been worked out whereby relief can be afforded for drainage systems installed by subdividers on behalf of municipalities, where this is required by the subdivision agreement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think I can say that the municipalities generally have been most ingenious in working out arrangements so that the tax exemption is available.
I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary would share some of those ingenious techniques with the house some time so that we will at least know how they operate?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
Paragraph 8 agreed to.
On paragraph 9.

Mr. Chairman, I am rather glad to see a second cabinet minister present, because I was a little worried over the fact that we might be wasting our time here if we were persuasive and found that we did not have the necessary executive quorum to pass amendments. It would not have been very worth while.
I wonder whether the words in this paragraph mean just what they say. I wonder whether, when we see the bill, there is going to be some restriction of which no notice is

given here. This paragraph refers to furbearing animals. I presume this means all fur-bearing animals and would not bear the type of restriction that I think has hitherto applied, namely fur-bearing animals whose pelts have commercial value. I think this is the phrase in the schedule. In other words, I hope that when the bill comes down it will include all fur-bearing animals.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; there is no doubt about that, Mr. Chairman. What is in fact happening is a consolidation of certain items as they appear in the present schedule to the Excise Tax Act.
So that the present restriction on the feeds themselves, which is restricted to animals whose pelts have commercial value, will be removed in the new schedule?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I have some difficulty here in finding the item in the farm and forest schedule for feeds and feed supplements generally in agriculture. I know they are there, and of course I should find them in some of the tariff items. The free tariff items are also exempt from the sales tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. If the hon. member will look at the fifth line from the bottom of page 28 of the Excise Tax Act consolidation, he will find stock conditioners, condiments, and feed supplements in addition to poultry, cattle and other stock feeds.
Yes.
Just one question. Will this exemption also apply to fur-bearing animals which are kept in a zoo?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, wherever they may be kept. Indeed, it will apply to persons who might be feeding fur-bearing animals in a state of nature.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 10.
This paragraph has to do with hardware for doors and sash. Presumably this will include hardware for cupboard doors?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Whether made on site or not? Hitherto I believe if the hardware was made on site it perhaps was exempt but if made in a factory, prefabricated, it bore tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hardware made on site in the past has been exempt; if made in a manufacturing establishment it was taxable.
I do not understand this paragraph. Is the purport of it to remove the tax from the prefabricated sash and door hardware?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The situation was that anyone who was buying a door upon which the hardware was installed was getting the hardware free of tax, but if he was buying the hardware separately and then installing it with the door he was paying the tax.
What will be the situation after the passing of this amendment? We are still not too clear on that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What this does is level it out, and they both get the benefit of those items which are specifically exempt.
By that the parliamentary secretary means that sash and door hardware used in new construction is exempt from tax; is that it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; only if specifically mentioned in the act, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall paragraph 11 carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 12.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as indicated on page 2 of the appendix to Votes and Proceedings for Friday, May 6, there is an amendment to this paragraph. Without reading it, perhaps I might just refer the committee to that page where the amendment is set out in full and ask my colleague, the Postmaster General, to move this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
move:
That paragraph 12 of the Excise Tax Act resolution be deleted and the following substituted therefor:

Excise Tax Act
not including coverings or containers designed for dispensing goods for sale or designed for repeated use other than
