speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall paragraph 12 as amended carry?
No, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Nickel Belt was rising.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, I expected that you would read the clause and ask if we were prepared to have it carried. Would the minister tell the committee if oil tanks are exempt as before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, there is a special exemption in the act now for oil tanks.
And that remains?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, this amendment does not affect that.

There was no reference to them in the amendment and I gathered that possibly they would still be covered. In the face of this amendment we are brought back to certain matters which we had occasion to discuss this morning with relation to another item. If I ask the minister certain questions and make certain remarks it is with the thought that the amendment now proposed brings about a situation whereby the small home owner will be subjected to additional taxation to satisfy the needs of the Minister of Finance. I have reference particularly to containers for bottled gas which are sold to home owners in many communities for the purpose of heating and operating other facilities in the home. Bottled gas is used in many cases because it is possibly cheaper than electricity or oil, and therefore in this amendment the government is striking directly again at the small home owner. Bottled gas is used by people who can only afford to live in a trailer or a very small home, and if hon. members will travel throughout their constituencies they will realize that that is so. People who have to keep their living costs as low as possible are the ones who use manufactured bottled gas.
There is also the question of discrimination involved in this provision, for the Minister of Finance has just confessed in answer to my question that oil tanks are exempt from taxation. It is obvious from the construction of

Excise Tax Act
this new clause, which was read by the chairman a moment ago, that bottled gas containers are not exempt from taxation and thus people who are trying to keep their living costs at a minimum are now faced with an additional tax. I do not blame the person who sells the bottled gas for adding the additional tax to the price he charges the person purchasing the gas. He has figured that he can provide the gas and equipment at a certain price and therefore he cannot assume the cost of the additional tax imposed by the government without passing it on to the consumer. The reason for the amendment would appear to be that the minister has had a change of mind in the last few months. Undoubtedly the amendment he proposed and which was passed clearly indicates that the minister has had a change of mind. But in no way did he bring about, through his amendment, a solution to the problem of the people in this country who are interested in the manufacture of bottled gas. The reason I say that lies in the section which indicates that the container is exempt only if it is not designed for repeated use. I presume that the container for bottled gas is definitely designed for repeated use. It can be exchanged, and on occasion it is exchanged.
I should like to impress the minister with the fact he should not impose this new tax on home owners since we have already seen a few examples this morning of taxation which affected the home owner. I should like also to bring to his attention representations which I have received from my area, and no doubt other members have also received representations. The notification which these manufacturers received when the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech was that from that date forward the containers would not be exempted. Undoubtedly publicity was given to that fact and the minister must have received representations which resulted in this amendment of May 6. This would indicate he was trying to satisfy some of the representations, but I fail to see why the minister would decide to satisfy the representations of some people and not others. People have attempted to ascertain the significance the resolution, mentioned in the budget speech and further amended on May 6, would have on their operations.
We find that since April 1 people have been paying a tax on these containers for bottled gas. I should like to ask the minister if those people who have already paid the tax on these containers will have their money refunded. Will he make sure that these people now come under the proper rule which the committee is asked to adopt? People have written to the department and, of course, since the resolution was presented by the

Minister of Finance, the department was obligated to inform them that a new tax of 11 per cent had been imposed and these people have been paying this tax. However, on May 6 some people were exempted from the payment and this fact has been confirmed by the amendment which has just been passed by the committee. Those people who had been paying the tax during the month of April were removed from the list of taxpayers and were advised of this fact, indirectly or otherwise. However, the trailer owners and small home owners are faced with a situation where they are told today by the Minister of Finance that they must continue to pay this additional tax of 11 per cent.
There is a company in Sudbury known as the Sudbury Bottled Gas Company, and after having been advised by the company in Hamilton that the tax had to be paid they were worried about what would happen today. I am asking the Minister of Finance if he will not take a second look at this situation and be prepared to make sure that this one group of citizens is not called upon to bear heavier burdens than others in similar businesses, those selling oil and oil furnaces. Recently I received a letter which I believe would give a much clearer picture of the situation than I could give. It was written by the owner of this company I just mentioned, Mr. John Martin, and is addressed to me. I should like to make reference to at least some of the paragraphs, but not take the time of the committee by reading it in full. The letter reads in part as follows:
Just because the government in power requires revenue, it does not justify a form of legal extortion in the sense of a piece of legislation or otherwise, to acquire this revenue.
I feel very strongly about this subject and as a small business operation, the ramification from this piece of legislation, which I understand is not in this year's budget, but which is in effect, from the letter that I provided you with, is allowed to continue, it is going to deal a severe blow to the home heating, cooking, hot water, and domestic industry.
Mr. Martin makes a further reference to the fact that the people interested in oil services are obtaining these oil tanks free of tax as a result of the amendment which was suggested on May 6. It would seem to me, therefore, that there must be an explanation the minister could give which would help members of this committee in understanding why certain citizens are being taxed in certain businesses and not in others. Furthermore, I should like to inform the minister that the people who are paying this tax levied on bottled gas are the consumers. Reference has been made on several occasions lately to the fact that the consumer is the person who will furnish the revenue resulting from this tax. Surely if the government requires

this money there must be a medium by which they can obtain it and whereby the consumer and the small home owner will not be the ones who furnish it. There must be a more equitable system by which certain moneys can be obtained than by having the burden rest solely on the shoulders of the persons to whom this amendment refers. I trust the minister will immediately give a clear-cut explanation for the discrimination that exists under this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this proposed amendment to the act does not create discrimination. On the contrary, it removes it. It does none of the things the hon. gentleman has said of it. I am afraid the hon. member has been guilty of some gross exaggeration in what he has had to say.
In the first place, the Excise Tax Act applies a tax, the sales tax, generally to all commodities. Then the scheme of the act contemplates certain named exemptions set out in certain schedules to the act. If there is to be an exemption, therefore, it must be found in explicit terms in the schedule to the act. This has been the scheme of this act from the outset. It has been the policy of parliament to write certain specific exemptions into the act, such as, many food products, building materials and other commodities, in the case of which parliament thought there was some special reason for exempting them from a tax that is otherwise of completely general application.
Now the question concerns coverings, the usual coverings on goods that are exempt. What is to happen to those? Obviously the principle that ought to be followed there is to determine whether the covering is one that finds its end use with the sale of the particular exempt commodity or whether, on the other hand, it is a covering that goes back to the supplier and is then used in future sales. In other words, is it a case of a covering like, we will say, the cardboard cover or the cellophane cover on a box of corn flakes or is it a container that is capable of further use, one that goes back to the producer or supplier for repeated use? Obviously there is no reason why coverings that are capable of repeated use should, in principle, be exempt from a general tax. That has been the principle that has been given broad recognition in this act for many years now.
In the experience of the Department of National Revenue which is charged with the responsibility for administration and enforcement of this provision difficulties have arisen. There have been many cases in which it appears that attempts have been made to extend the area of exemption in cases where
Excise Tax Act
there is no proper case for exemption. This provision was introduced with a view to meeting that situation. It is a provision that is necessary in order to block what were found to be certain loopholes and to remove discriminations; and it is in keeping with the principle that has been recognized by the act, as I believe, ever since its inception.
Mention has been made of the fact that the original resolution itself has been amended. Yes, Mr. Chairman; it has been amended, again in the interests of clarification and in certain clear cases to put beyond all question the exemption that exists. I would therefore point out that the amendment that has just been adopted by the committee is one which is relieving in its effect. If you will note what the amendment does you will find that it applies this exemption to what are called the usual coverings of foods. You have the covering for fruits and vegetables, eggs, butter and cheese, ice cream, bread, milk and cream bottles, milk and cream cans.
They were all exempt previously.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose there is to make it quite clear that what are the usual coverings of these particular foods are to retain that exemption. The hon. member now goes further and raises the case of the coverings of propane gas. Let me make it perfectly clear that here there is nothing that proposes to apply the sales tax to any covering for propane gas that comes into use in a particular sale. The sales tax under this provision will apply in relation to propane gas and apply only in the case of cylinders which contain propane gas which are used in the sale and then go back to the supplier and are capable of being used over and over again. I submit that, having regard to the application of the sales tax to all other manner of coverings that are capable of and intended to be for repeated use, there is no reason at all why there should be an exemption in the case of these cylinders that contain propane gas.
The hon. member pictures this provision as doing some harm to the home owner. Mr. Chairman, that is an unrecognizable exaggeration. If the home owner purchases propane gas in containers that are not returned for repeated use on the part of the suppliers, then the sales tax has no application to that covering whatsoever. But if the purchase is made in larger quantities that call for the use of a cylinder to contain the gas and that cylinder is the kind that goes back and is used over and over again, perhaps 50 times or 100 times, then I say it is not in keeping with the principle of the act that that cylinder in its repeated use should be exempt from the sales tax.

Excise Tax Act
This is a fair proposal. It is a proposal that is in keeping with the general principle of the act. I think it is a most far fetched plea to say that this has something to do with the cost of homes or is somehow related to the home owner. Mr. Chairman, this is a tax that applies on all suppliers who use that particular cylinder over and over again.
We are being asked to assume that this is going to create an imposition on the home owner. Mr. Chairman, can you take seriously the suggestion that the application of the sales tax on that particular article is going to create an increase in cost to the home owner when that article is used over and over again, perhaps 50, 100 or 150 times? To use the case of a home owner in order to mount an attack on this provision is surely the most far fetched resort to oratory that we can well imagine in this situation.
This is a necessary clarifying provision, a provision that is in keeping with the principle of this act, a principle that has been recognized for many years.

I rise on a question of privilege. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance would permit me just to interrupt proceedings for a minute or two in order to ask the leader of the house whether it would be convenient to the government to take the estimates of the Post Office Department instead of those of the Department of Transport at four o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think that arrangement would be quite satisfactory. I believe the various parties in the house have been informed of the change suggested by the hon. member. The government is quite prepared to go along with that idea.

Speaking on behalf of this group, in order to indicate our willingness always to co-operate to suit the convenience of hon. gentlemen of the opposition, may I say that we are pleased to agree with the suggestion.
I thank the house leader.

I must apologize to the minister for arriving a little bit late. He may have answered the point that I wish to raise. I listened carefully to the representations made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt. However, this exemption has caused a great deal of confusion over a good number of years. I remember receiving representations as far back as six years ago, especially from manufacturers of containers that are used in the small fruits industry and of containers used by those who produce our vegetables. The amendment calls for these

containers to be taxable unless they are delivered and sold with the goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member. He indicated that he came in late. He may not be aware of the fact that the committee has already adopted an amendment that makes perfectly clear the exemption in favour of barrels, boxes, baskets, crates and bags for packaging fruits and vegetables.
I want to raise a point of order. It is not my understanding that we have passed the amendment. We have received the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amendment was passed. The hon. member for Nickel Belt was speaking on the paragraph as amended but the amendment that was introduced by the Postmaster General at my request has been adopted.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is being discussed now is the clause as amended-
As amended, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -or paragraph 12 as amended.

I want to be clear on this matter. Does that mean that wooden or cardboard containers for fruits and vegetables will not be liable to taxation even though they may be returned and used over and over again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The minister states that this is not a new principle, and that it has been in existence for a long time. It is my contention that this is something new. The bottled gas operators were not paying excise tax on the container before they were advised in the budget speech that they would be doing so according to the new resolution then mentioned on March 31 which has now been amended.
It is new taxation.
By so stating the minister forces me to read further from this letter which I was endeavouring to abbreviate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me give all assistance to the hon. member's desire to abbreviate. Let me say at once that I was speaking about the principle of the act. What we have dealt with here is an anomaly. What the hon. member is referring to is an anomalous situation in the light of the act and we are in the amendment as proposed in the resolution, following a course which

is in keeping with the principle of the act and which will eliminate what was an anomaly. There should not have been an exemption in that case. It is a highly discriminatory situation if that were a permitted exemption. I was speaking of the principle of this act. An anomaly did exist. This provision will eliminate that anomaly and vindicate the principle which applies generally.

The Minister of Finance must have a new definition of "anomaly" because I do not see any way in which the government can suggest that an oil tank purchased from an oil dealer should be regarded differently from the circumstances which arise when a home owner goes to a propane bottling firm and purchases the equipment required to service propane gas. If the container cost $40 he would pay $45 because the man furnishing the service would have to ascertain that he has purchased a sufficient number of containers to satisfy the number of new customers.
Therefore, a home owner will pay on the installation of the service of propane gas an additional tax of 11 per cent on the container, whereas a person who instals an oil system will not pay a 11 per cent tax on the oil tank which the supplier will furnish on the purchase of the oil heating system. This is discrimination. The minister said he intends to do away with discrimination but, in fact, he has only created discrimination in the administration of this exemption which previously put both suppliers on an even footing. Today they find they are in different positions.
Now that the minister has made the proposition he has I will read a letter which a certain firm had mimeographed and sent to the bottlers of propane gas so they would know about the 11 per cent tax which would be added to the cost of the containers, a tax which is borne by the home owner, and I have heard no one say to the contrary in this house. This letter is from Engineering Products of Canada Limited, it is addressed to the Sudbury Bottled Gas Company and is dated May 26, 1960. It reads:
Reference is made to your letter of May 19, 1960, in which you advise you were "shocked" at the addition of 11 per cent F.S.T. to the basic price of your cylinders.
Enclosed please find a photostatic copy of a letter from the customs and excise branch of the federal government. After reading same and a covering letter we are sending to all our customers, you will realize the matter is beyond our control.
This firm went to the expense of having a mimeographed letter prepared to be sent to all the persons with whom they had dealings. It continues:
Numerous representations have been made to the government. However, last week a delegation
Excise Tax Act
was turned down flat, with the result the 11 per cent F.S.T. is here to stay.
The next time you have a talk with your friend Mr. John Diefenbaker you can discuss it in detail with him, and with your forceful nature and argumentative capabilities you might be able to have him rescind it. Sorry John, but we have no other option than charge this sales tax on all cylinders we sell.
This person who was inquiring about the situation in the area in which he is trying to furnish this service finds that the people who are dealing with oil heating equipment obtain their containers for the oil which they have to sell upon the installation of the service free of tax. Against that we have no quarrel, and I am sure that Mr. John Martin, to whom the letter I read was addressed, and who has made representations to myself and to the government on this matter, has no quarrel with the fact that other people are exempt from tax. But he certainly has a complaint against the government on the ground that the government discriminates against him. I must go on to read a few more paragraphs of the letter from the Sudbury Bottled Gas Company which I was endeavouring to abbreviate a few minutes ago.
I would like to further quote that the Milne Steel Fabricating Company, Hamilton, Ontario are selling to Groom-Callahan Wholesale Hardware and distributors in the Sudbury area, 200 gallon oil tanks which are parallel to our propane tanks and are used almost identically for the same purpose as our propane tanks are.
On May 16, 1960, Groom-Callahan made a purchase of oil tanks and there was no 11 per cent sales tax levied. This would indicate to me that there is direct discrimination against our industry and which I request you, Mr. Godin, and authorize you, on my behalf, that I personally charge the government with the responsibility of not running the affairs of this country properly.
Could it be possible that there is some pressure or collusion, and this is only a suggestion, that the natural gas is putting the pressure on? I am sure that you will use your good offices to convey this message to the Prime Minister and those concerned.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to make representations which I have been asked to make with regard to this matter. Judging by these letters I believe the complaints must be numerous, and that discrimination exists. I am sure Mr. Martin has no quarrel against Groom-Callahan for not having to pay excise tax on the oil tanks. Surely, however, it is obvious to all hon. members that the Minister of Finance should try to find a way of giving similar treatment to similar types of business. It seems to me that once again this government is found lacking in that it has loaded additional taxes on consumers in one sphere only, to provide for we do not know what.
Undoubtedly it was the intention of the minister to do away with an exemption which

Excise Tax Act
existed. Then came about the volte face of May 6, to which I referred this morning, when an effort was made by the minister to patch up some of the mistakes made in his budget resolutions on March 21. Those were not good enough, and I say the Minister of Finance should reconsider the position of the government and not burden the consumer with this additional tax which discriminates against businesses of great similarity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member must be a master of exaggeration. He has undertaken to put an interpretation on this particular resolution which bears no resemblance to the facts. He is talking about discrimination, and he uses the yardstick of fuel oil tanks. The schedule to the act makes a specific provision in relation to fuel oil tanks. The exemption is written in these words:
Fuel oil tanks where used for furnaces for the heating of buildings and connected directly to such furnaces.
It will be seen at once that the gist of that exemption is that the fuel oil tank is installed in the house, and it stays there. This exemption does not apply to a container in which fuel oil is delivered to the home and taken away again for repeated use. What we are talking about here is the matter of coverings of goods. The hon. member has not at all followed or attempted to follow, evidently, the clear principle that is inscribed in the act in this regard. What we are talking about are coverings on the one hand which come to their end use with the delivery of the goods and on the other hand coverings that, after delivery, are returned to the supplier and used over and over again in the case of future deliveries.
The fuel oil tank is a very clear case of the first category, namely the delivery and the end use, and there is only one purchase by the home owner. The fuel tank is installed and that is the end of the matter. It is not a case of the fuel tank going back to the supplier of the fuel oil every time it is empty. The other case is that of the cylinder in which gas is delivered and if that cylinder is capable of repeated use and after delivery of the gas the cylinder is returned to the supplier and then used by him over and over again, the exemption should not apply.
If the gas is delivered in a container which meets its end use with that particular delivery and is not returned then the exemption applies. That is the principle of the act. It is a clear principle and the present resolution is completely in accord with that principle. What the hon. gentleman has cited is not a situation that indicates discrimination raised by this new resolution. He has pointed very

clearly to the reason for the anomaly that existed in the case of certain of these cylinders that were being used, returned to the supplier and used over and over again. The hon. gentleman has pointed out why that anomaly crept in. It is completely out of accord with the principle of this act in relation to the taxation on coverings.

Mr. Chairman, surely the act speaks for itself. This section has been in the act in specific language for some considerable time. The minister is confusing the anomalies and the principles he has in mind as a new minister with what he thinks he wants to propose for the first time in connection with a method of taxation. The point is that this article did not bear taxation under the law as it existed under the previous administration. The minister has new ideas and wants to bring into taxation for the first time articles of this kind. The exemption was written into the act. It is found in the appendix and reads as follows:
Usual coverings to be used exclusively for covering goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture of such coverings.
The principle is that natural gas, electricity and these heating elements are commodities that were not subject to the consumption tax under the law and the minister wants now to change it so these commodities will bear tax. This is a new tax on this type of article.
The language of the act has been tested. It is my understanding that there was a recent case of appeal to the tariff board. It was made quite clear by the tariff board which looked upon the language of the statute judicially that the language was clear and plain as presented by the previous administration. The minister now proposes to change it and what we have is a new tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member must have been reading from different reasons for judgment on the part of the tariff board than those which other people read because the tariff board did not find it at all clear. It found it a very difficult provision because the present provision is so lacking in clarity and has opened loopholes for anomalies such as the one that has been pointed out. The need for amendment of it has become quite clear.

Perhaps I do not understand the wording or perhaps the minister is not clear in his understanding of it. The test of the resolution is not the one the minister suggested and I do not think the courts would support the view he advances. The test is to be found in the words "designed for repeated use".

It is all very well to say that bottled gas containers are returned to the company for repeated use but in what way does that alter the position of the home owner? When he makes a contract with a propane gas company he must pay the cost of the first container and will therefore be subject to the payment of the 11 per cent tax on the article. Under the new resolution the home owner will have to pay the 11 per cent tax if he is a bottle gas user whereas another person with other equipment may be free of tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I am not capable of making this any plainer. If hon. gentlemen opposite persist in misreading the effect of this I am afraid I cannot do anything about it. The language of the amendment clearly contains the expression "designed for repeated use". That is the principle. I have repeated that several times. I do not wish to waste the committee's time by trying to clarify this through further repetition. I will merely draw the hon. member's attention to these words which contain the gist of the test.
The hon. member talks about the home owner bearing the burden of the tax. It is not without significance that the letter the hon. gentleman read and which undertook to apply strictures against the government was a letter not written out of solicitude for the home owner but a letter as between the manufacturer of the cylinder and the company that sells the propane gas. To take that and make out of it an argument that this is going to hurt the home owner is to indulge in an improper application of imagination to the situation. To say that in the sale of these coverings a sales tax is not to be applied in keeping with the application of sales tax to all other coverings of similar nature and to say that this is going to create some liability on the part of the home owner is to fly in the teeth of the facts.
The cylinder is acquired by the supplier of the propane gas. It is going to be used again and again. That is the essence of the matter. To say that this is going to place an 11 per cent tax on the home owner is surely overtaxing the credence and the imagination of any hon. member of this committee.
What about the milk cans we use?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The case is quite clear there. There is a specific exemption in the case of the coverings of food. Surely that is very clear. The committee has already recognized that in adopting the amendment to the resolution. To say that this is going to affect the home owner when it is a matter between the supplier of the cylinder and the company that sells the propane gas and to
Excise Tax Act
make out of that a suggestion that there is going to be some burden thrown on the home owner is overtaxing the imagination of any of us.
Paragraph as amended agreed to.
On paragraph 13.

Would the minister give us an explanation of this. I know the hon. gentleman offered an explanation on budget night but I find it difficult on reading the language of the amendment to determine if it is accomplishing what the minister said was his intention. On March 31, 1960, as reported at page 2683 of Hansard the minister said:
In order to avoid the possibility of misunderstanding I shall mention a comparatively minor amendment intended to prevent private individuals who purchase yachts from avoiding the imposition of sales tax in respect of the materials that are included. This will not affect the commercial shipyards, which will continue as before to purchase materials for the construction of ships free of sales tax under licence.
I have received correspondence from some ship architects and they point out that as one reads this proposed change it would appear that the word "construction" is taken out and if a ship of over ten tons is to be constructed, it would appear that it no longer would enjoy the benefit of the sales tax exemption which has hitherto been in the appendix.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I mentioned this particular proposal specifically in the budget speech because I hoped thereby to avoid misunderstanding. It is not that the item itself is intrinsically so important as to warrant special mention, but it was simply a matter of avoiding a possible misunderstanding pending the period when in this committee any necessary explanation might be given.
This paragraph of the resolution proposes that the word "construction" be deleted from the present exemption. This is intended for purposes of clarification and to obviate attempts by individuals to have private yachts built on a sales tax exempt basis and thus obtain an unintended relief from the tax.
The word "construction" in the exemption is not necessary for the shipbuilder, as he can always use his manufacturer's licence to purchase materials and equipment entering into the manufacture of his vessels on a tax free basis. However, the wording of the exemption played into the hands of the individual who wanted to build a pleasure craft for his own use. The word "construction" in the exemption enabled that individual to purchase materials without payment of the tax and then turn them over to a shipbuilder who would custom build the ship for him, thus avoiding payment of the tax on the

Excise Tax Act
materials as well as on the finished craft. If the same individual bought a finished craft from the builder he would pay sales tax on his entire purchase, namely on the completed vessel.
The amended exemption will not affect the sales tax status of ships built in Canada and purchased by non-residents; they would still be exempt from sales tax as exports.
The exemption from sales tax for "boats bona fide purchased by fishermen for use in fisheries, and articles and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture, equipment or repair of such boats" is not being changed. In other words, Mr. Chairman, to sumarize, so far as the interests of fishermen are concerned, there will be no change created by this proposed amendment. In the case of bona fide shipbuilders there is no change, but this paragraph of the resolution will block a loophole of which some persons have made use.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Paragraph agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At this point may I ask my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to introduce the amendment which I indicated on May 6 and which appears on page 2 of the appendix to Votes and Proceedings of that day. It is to insert a new paragraph 14, and to number the subsequent paragraphs of the resolution accordingly. It is to introduce a new exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
I move:
That the Excise Tax Act resolution be amended by inserting a new paragraph immediately following paragraph 13 thereof to read as follows:
"14. That drainage, waste and vent copper tubing from two inches to six inches in diameter, with a wall thickness from .040 to .083 of an inch, for non-pressure applications, and fittings therefor, be exempt from sales tax." and that the subsequent paragraphs of the resolution be renumbered accordingly.
Will the minister give an explanation, perhaps indicating the common use of this material.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This new paragraph proposes that copper tube or pipe and fittings thereof sold for use as waste and drain pipes and for providing a vent in plumbing fixtures be made exempt from sales tax. This kind of copper tube or pipe is an alternative to cast iron soil pipe in plumbing installations in buildings. Cast iron soil pipe has been exempt from sales tax from the time the exemption was first introduced for building materials. In recent years copper has replaced cast iron soil pipe to a large extent, and the proposed amendment recognizes changing techniques and use of materials in the building industry.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, this, I think, can be looked upon as a matter of removing the discrimination that exists now in the light of changing use. I think the committee will realize now that having regard to the extension of the use of copper pipe this type of installation should enjoy the same kind of tax treatment as the cast iron soil pipe in plumbing installations.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Paragraph 14, renumbered 15, agreed to.
Paragraph 15, renumbered 16, agreed to.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Mr. Chairman, is it the intention to call the individual items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the individual items are called I daresay there will be a lot of calling. I do not think that has been the practice in times past. We shall do just whatever the committee wishes. There are, however, seven resolutions involved here. We are not dealing with seven paragraphs of one resolution, Mr. Chairman, but with seven different resolutions. What I suggest, Mr. Chairman, is that the individual resolutions be called in the order in which they appear here. When you come to some of the individual resolutions which apply to a considerable number of tariff items, perhaps it would suffice to call the page in the printed pamphlet of ways and means resolutions. I doubt whether it will be necessary to call each individual item.

I recall that in the past the chairman went down quickly and recited the item number. Perhaps it will be sufficient to call the page number. We will try it. Will you call page 9, which is part of resolution No. 2?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resolution No. 1 is carried.
Will you call page 9?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

First of all, in connection with this fairly large package, will the minister indicate which of the items which are being changed were negotiated through GATT in the GATT tariffs in order to adjust the textile

tariffs? Perhaps he might indicate to the committee which of the items concerned which involve concessions in those negotiations are of relative importance and which have some monetary importance in the pattern of volume of imports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolution No. 2 contains what might be described as the textile package. By this I mean that it contains the tariff changes required to implement the various tariff board reports on textiles to which I referred in the budget speech. It also contains other changes resulting from the textile negotiations, to which the hon. member referred.
As I mentioned in the budget speech, the revised textile schedule recommended by the board involved both increases and reductions in duty. However, the increases, of which the most important relates to coloured cotton fabrics, somewhat overbalance the decreases. Hence in order to conclude renegotiation of our commitments under GATT, for most of the items in question were bound under GATT, we found it necessary to reduce about a score of Canadian tariff rates on items outside the textile field. To the extent that the Canadian textile industry is on balance receiving some additional protection as recommended by the tariff board, this is being matched by reductions in other fields. In other words, that was the compensation that had to be given to the other countries to obtain their agreement to the increases under the provisions of GATT.
As I indicated in the budget speech, some of these reductions were requested by Canadian industry while others involved small reductions from relatively high rates of duty and in these cases it is not thought that the reductions should materially damage the industries affected. When the hon. member asks me how many of these items are affected by GATT, the answer is most of them, practically all of them.

I was also curious as to which of the many items might have the greatest importance, that is, would involve a greater amount of trade. Am I right in thinking that on this page, by way of an example of tariff reduction, item 187e, which deals with negative film for 16 millimetre motion picture cameras, might perhaps be an important item of import from the United States, would it be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not regarded as a very large item. Imports come mostly from the United States, but it is not regarded as a very large item.

It is several months since the minister gave notice of his intention to 79951-0-295
Customs Tariff
reduce the most favoured nation tariff from 20 per cent to 15 per cent. Have his officers reported to him any change in retail prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.
When I looked at item 236 on this page I could not see any reason for it appearing here and I wonder what the change is that brings it into the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I commended the minister yesterday for the practice of having the amendments to the budget resolutions printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings as soon as he found it was possible to do so and had decided it was necessary to make amendments. I would also commend him for including a brief explanation as to the reason for this amendment

Customs Tariff
but I must say that the explanation given does not seem to be completely satisfactory. It reads:
The proposed change in wording is for purposes of clarification.
As I come from a mining district I wonder whether it is not more than that because I would think that the amendment is considerably less attractive than the original proposal. New words are inserted in the amendment which are restrictive, namely "but not including roof bolts or washers or nuts therefor".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was never
intended that the item should include the material to which the hon. member has referred, and this is simply a clarification.

Mr. Chairman, this whole resolution deals with items in the tariff that are bound by GATT. How much flexibility has the minister in making amendments with respect to items that are related to GATT? He indicated to the house on budget night that certain trading had been done and he was able to bring in a new schedule in connection with quite a number of items. He now proposes to amend some of those items. What flexibility and freedom has he in a trading matter of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it that the hon. member is asking about future negotiations?

No, I am saying that the minister indicated that practically all these items are items that needed to be changed because of adjustments that had to be made in compensation for requests that the Canadian government made with respect to textile items that were bound by GATT. The minister reported to the house on budget night that he was now in a position to bring in these amendments and that they represented the result of a fair amount of negotiation. Since then the minister has introduced amendments to some of these items and I am wondering how much freedom he has in amending and whether he has to go back to the GATT country before he can bring in such an amendment?

This means that the majority of them are obliged to go down to the central post office. This may not seem to be a particular burden but I should like to point out that in a community such as Sioux Lookout or Hornepayne-which happen to be communities in which I am interested-these communities were built at a time when real estate was bitten off in rather large chunks. From many points in Hornepayne it is well over a mile to the post office and in Sioux Lookout it is a distance of 1J miles to 2 miles for many of the people who reside in that place.
It has been suggested to me by the people of these communities that the post office authorities might consider establishing the kind of boxes that are used for suburban mail delivery in suburban areas such as we have in the south part of Ottawa. We have not reached the stage of door to door deliveries. However we might have some system like that. This kind of decentralized distribution would be of great advantage.

how this list is compiled, but I have tried to make use of it and I find that it seems to be remarkably out of date. I can give an example of two communities where I took names. I sent mail-call it propaganda if you wish-to all the names on the list. I got a remarkable number back, and I discovered on checking that some of the people to whom I had sent were university students who had been employed there a year ago; they were just there for the summer, but somehow when the list was compiled their names were still on it. It is a method of evening up the

balance. If there is unfairness in having to wait for mail, it seems to me that this unfairness should be shifted round in the community so that each part shares it equally.

I hope later on to have the opportunity of bringing up a further point. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to clearing up the question of the letters marked "personal and confidential"-an endorsement which appears on the correspondence of almost all members of parliament. I have a hunch that this is one of the most broken labels in Canada, and I would like an explanation of why the minister introduced this practice or why he carries it on.

In the few remarks I have to make on this subject I should like first of all to compliment the postmen and the rural mail carriers who battle the elements to deliver the mail as best they can to the Canadian people and who seldom get the credit they deserve.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General once again the very bad service they get in the North Surrey and Delta areas of British Columbia. In these fast growing areas with a population of between 60,000 and 70,000 I understand on good authority it takes at least three days to get first class local mail delivered and up to 10 days to get second and third class local mail. I am told that a letter mailed in Clover-dale to the town of Newton takes a minimum of four days. The ex-reeve of Surrey has

told me on different occasions when he was reeve of Surrey and lived in Newton he mailed letters to his home and it was at least four days before they were delivered.
I have in my hand a letter posed in White Rock on January 2, addressed to the local member of the legislature in Surrey, British Columbia. According to the postmark it was delivered on January 12, ten days later. The distance involved is approximately 10 or 12 miles. It may be said that this is an isolated case but I know it is not. I have received hundreds of complaints about similar delays in that area. The historic pony express of the last century, I am sure, gave better service than we often get in North Surrey.
According to the Stevenson Kellogg industrial survey, and the one conducted by the Western Development and Power Corporation it is predicted that by 1970 the area known as Whalley will have a population of over
70,000	and the area known as Newton will have a population of over 50,000. Approximately 45 years ago a post office was established in the Newton area. True it was small with a public lobby of about 100 square feet, with 50 post office boxes and a waiting list of some 200 but with an expanding population which is now over 20,000 various local organizations have been clamouring for years for better facilities. These organizations include the chamber of commerce, the Canadian Legion, the Canadian ratepayers' association and other groups.
The postal officials in Vancouver, aware of conditions, went out and investigated. In company with the reeve they selected property for a new building. Plans were drawn and the former minister of public works announced that a new building was to be erected, construction of which was to commence last fall. You can readily understand the consternation and feeling of disappointment of the people of Newton when the Postmaster General announced that they were not to get a new post office but that he was going to close the existing one and their mail was to be delivered to New Westminster. The minister announced that a subpost office to handle stamps and money orders would be opened in the back of a drug or shoe store. This retrograde step was vigorously opposed by the organizations to which I have referred and by many residents of the community who had worked for years to get better postal facilities and service.
In view of the strong protests the postal officials from Vancouver met with the municipal council and stated that the present plan was drawn up by their field representative but they had an open mind and did not wish to go against the wishes of the people.

Similar statements were made by the Postmaster General in letters he sent in reply to protests he received.
I am at a loss to know how the organizations could put up a stronger protest but the department ignoring the assurances they had given are now proceeding with their plan. In effect, the department have said, "This is the postal service we have decided is best for you and it is what you are going to take regardless of how you feel about it."
At the same meeting with council the officials stated that the subpostal station now located at Whalley was quite adequate to service this large population. However, they later admitted it was much too small and that they had been pressing for larger quarters for several years. From this it would appear they were endeavouring to mislead the public. It is apparent the Postmaster General has again been misled when he states in a letter:
The time may come when it will be desirable to have a central post office in North Surrey, but such a post office is not required now and the time at which it will be necessary lies a long way in the future.
It is utter nonsense to say that a post office is not required. To support my argument let me read from an article which appeared in the December 22, 1959 issue of the Vancouver Sun:
Mailmen Criticize Inadequate Space-Newton Ratepayers Backed in Drive for Post Office
Newton ratepayers have found unexpected support in their campaign to have a post office built in the South Surrey area.
Their allies-unhappy rural mail carriers.
The men who deliver mail on the rural routes south of Whalley complain that they've been shuffled into inadequate quarters for the Christmas rush.

"Because there wasn't enough room for us to work in the North Surrey post office, they put us into the unfinished Whalley Legion building.
When we started last Monday, there were no lights and no toilet facilities. We had to string our own lights. They hooked up one toilet Tuesday, but there are men and women working there, and it isn't enough."
The rural mail carriers say it isn't the local postmaster's fault.
"He's doing all he can with too little space. It's the post office people in Ottawa."
The carriers would also like to know what happened to plans to build a postal station at Newton.
"We heard that the land had been purchased and that money had been allotted for a building."
The only reason we were able to get the inadequate space in the Legion building is because they aren't ready to open to the public yet. What's going to happen next year? We may be in tents, for all we know.
He concluded by saying that the planned Newton post office would have been perfect for the rural carriers to work from, and asked why the plans hadn't been carried out.

The minister must know in view of the number of protests that something is wrong with the postal service in this area. In my opinion what is needed is a postal substation in the Whalley district to handle the large volume of commercial and residential mail in the area and another one in Newton for distribution of the considerable volume of mail throughout this industrial community where many light industries are locating and where the British Columbia Telephone Company has established its central billing office for the whole Fraser valley which will create a considerable amount of mail. I suggest to the minister that he personally investigate the situation in these districts and talk to the people concerned in regard to the postal service they have been receiving rather than consulting with some of his officials who have been leading him up the garden path. (Translation):

I wish to put the following questions to the Postmaster General: Why did Canada fail to issue a postage stamp in honour of refugees in 1960, while most other countries did so?
We know that 1960 is world refugee year. We also know that out of 40 million refugees, 15 million are still homeless.
Most stamps issued by other countries bear the symbol used by the United Nations, an uprooted tree.
By issuing a stamp, we would have made a charitable and humanitarian gesture. It seems to me that it would have been advisable for Canada to make known to all countries what it has done for world refugees and to point out the support given in the past and still being given to those outcasts of fortune.
Since many countries, 70 to be exact, have issued such a stamp, I ask the minister to tell us why Canada has not issued a refugee stamp.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief. Before asking the Postmaster General a few questions, as a former postmaster I should like to commend him, his deputy, the department and staff on the fine work that is being done and the splendid cooperation I have received, as well as others, in our daily inquiries and occasional problems.
My first question concerns salaries of a district director and area superintendent. These men have a big job to do. My second question is, what consideration has been given to my previous proposals that part-time assistants receive holidays with pay and superannuation benefits?
I was pleased to read in the budget speech of the increased salaries for civil servants. I hope that those working in the Post Office Department throughout Canada in the $6,000 bracket and under will be given first consideration.

The last time that this matter came up was May 27. At that time I raised what I thought was a very important question, and just about a minute before we adjourned that day the minister spent about half a minute in replying, and I admit that I said at that time I certainly was not satisfied with the reply. The last words that were said before adjournment were by myself, as found in Hansard at page 4306, where I said:
X should like to continue this discussion when these estimates come up again. The minister cannot get away with that type of fast answer on this important subject.
I am taking this opportunity to do what I said I was going to do and to ask for more consideration and a more detailed answer from the minister on a subject which I think is of the utmost importance.
I should like to thank the minister for having supplied us on May 27 with a cost ascertainment table for the fiscal year 1958-59. I should like to refer to this table. In a study of it we find that on first-class mail the Post Office Department made a profit of 1.827 cents per piece handled; on domestic air mail there was a profit of 17.665 cents per piece handled. But if you go to second-class mail you will find that on the transient there was a loss of 9.339 cents per piece and on publishers there was a loss of 4.084 cents per piece.
In an answer to a question during this session the minister himself stated that in 1958-59 disbursements over receipts amounted to $21,690,000 for newspapers and periodicals. The answer is to be found in Hansard of this year at page 1641.
I have maintained, and this group maintains, that it is not right in the Post Office

Department for the first-class ordinary and first-class air mail to be subsidizing the publishers; that is, the newspapers and the periodicals of this country. If it is not possible for that phase of the Post Office Department's operations to stand on its own feet and if it does require a subsidy, then that subsidy should not come from the users of ordinary and domestic air mail, it should come from the treasury of the Dominion of Canada. I made a statement to that effect when I spoke on May 27. What was the reply of the Postmaster General? I quote from page 4306 of Hansard of May 27. In the second column, half way down, this is what the minister had to say:
Finally, so far as publishers' mail is concerned, the distribution of publications, I would merely say to him that this operation shows up as a loss on the operating statement of the Post Office Department.
I want to emphasize what the minister said on May 27. I continue:
However, I take the view, and past governments have done, and I am sure succeeding governments will do, that we have a responsibility to enable the free and easy flow of information to all people in this country, and that magazines, books and newspapers, as well as other printed material of this sort, which helps to inform our people and raise the level of information, are entitled to consideration when postal rates are set.
The minister made it clear in that statement that as far as he is concerned as Postmaster General the delivery of newspapers, magazines and other publications of that nature, because it is a service of information to the people, has to be considered when the rates are set, and I am sure, therefore, he has no objection whatsoever-he is not suggesting any change-to their being subsidized, as his own figures prove, by the first-class ordinary mail and the domestic mail in Canada.
Perhaps the Postmaster General may ask why I said at that last minute on that day that he was not going to get away with that kind of a fast reply. I said that because I cannot understand-I think he owes a statement to the committee and to the people of Canada-why he has so completely changed his policy and point of view between the time he sat on this side of the house and becoming the Postmaster General. In the years that he sat on this side of the house he rose in his place and declared time after time that on this specific issue the carriage of newspapers, magazines and other publications should not be a charge on any other phase of postal deliveries; that if they required anything in the way of a subsidy it should come from the national treasury.
I think it is absolute hypocrisy, Mr. Chairman, for a man to sit for years on this side of the house and make declarations which

I took in honesty, in sincerity and in principle, and then when he has the power to do something about it to deny the principle which he has espoused. I am going to prove that that was the minister's principle by reading from his statement in Hansard. There are several of them but this is the most definite one. I refer to Hansard of 1953-54, volume II, January 14, 1954, at page 1117. The hon. member-he was not then a minister-started his speech on page 1115, at the top of the page, left-hand column. Here is what he had to say on the particular issue I am discussing, at page 1117, at the bottom of the first column of that page:
There is every reason in the world why this $131 million should be spent for what it is being spent for, but there is absolutely no reason why it should be charged to other users of the post office services. We should not load one class of mail with the costs of another class but we should rather bring out into the open and pay from general government revenues any special costs of this in the operation of a department.
How much more definite can a person be than the minister was when he made that statement at the time he sat on this side of the house? Yet when he is in a position to do something about the matter he no longer talks about it not being charged against other classes of mail or about it being paid out of general government revenues, something for which he fought so hard, wonderfully and eloquently when he sat on this side of the house.

he did not say anything in line with what he has said so often in the house in the past about the profits from other services not having to bear the deficiency incurred with respect to this service. The Postmaster General when in opposition was the chief critic of the Liberal postmaster general and I heard him say many times that that kind of cost should be met out of the general revenues of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make on the main item of the minister's estimates. I wish to draw the attention of the committee and more especially that of the minister to a situation in my province with regard to what are known as revenue post offices. For some strange reason the minister's department adopts the attitude that the small post office buildings in small settlements in the province, which were owned by the government of Newfoundland prior to union and hence were transferred to the government of Canada after union, should now be replaced by modern post office buildings which are most adequate to serve the needs of these particular areas. This often results in much larger settlements, some of them fairly close to these settlements which have the advantages of post office buildings, still having to put up with small inadequate postal services which in most cases are provided by the postmaster in his own premises.
I understand that the ruling of the Post Office Department is that where the revenue is in excess of $3,000 the Post Office Department will then consider the establishment of what is then known as a semi-staffed post office. If I am wrong I am sure the minister will correct me. Under these circumstances the Department of Public Works can be authorized to erect a new building. This might be very appropriate for certain areas of the country but in a province which is largely rural, although not in the sense of the word as it is understood elsewhere, and where post office services are most important and there are many small settlements spread along the extensive coastline, I submit that this rule should not necessarily apply.
I can give examples in my own constituency of certain areas. Granted that there may be three or four settlements in an area, but for all intents and purposes small postal facilities should be considered in the light of the aggregate amount of revenue. If this approach

Supply-Post Office
were adopted I think it would be found that we would be able to have decent postal facilities in the province.
Last year the Postmaster General visited our province and he saw some of these facilities at first hand. I am sure he fully realizes what I am talking about. We only have a very few urban areas in comparison with other provinces, and under this ruling of the Post Office Department whereby the revenue has to exceed a certain amount the settlements to which I have referred will never qualify for new post offices. I hope the Postmaster General in his wisdom will take this problem under advisement and will perhaps see fit to reopen the whole question of just when an area should qualify for a post office building because this service is a most important one and usually in these settlements the post office is the focal point or centre for the entire community. Because the Postmaster General has seen some at first hand I do not have to tell him about some of the premises that are being used by postmasters. They cannot provide better premises because in many cases the only revenue they get is a few hundred dollars a year. I submit to the Postmaster General that he should have his department look into this matter.

I should like to say a few words to support unreservedly every word uttered by the hon. member for St. John's East. X even tried to melt the hearts of my colleagues when we were in office on this very question and I have bombarded both the minister and the Minister of Public Works very persistently about this matter ever since the new government was formed. I should like to add one argument to what the hon. member said. In view of the fact that we have almost no rural free delivery in Newfoundland, which exists in all the other provinces-I have also urged the minister to look into that matter-what would be even more appreciated in most settlements is some relaxation of the rule that is applied on the mainland so that we will not have these anomalies where for historical reasons new post offices are built by the government in settlements much smaller than other settlements that are denied them simply because there was not one there before 1949. I might add that I am quite willing to make a bargain with the minister that if he will construct a building in Hare Bay I will be very happy if he has my defeated opponent make the announcement.

Mr. Chairman, may I just say a few words with regard to statements

made by the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) on May 27 last, when he made a long speech with lots of statistics. At the very outset of his remarks, the minister made a statement that does not show him up as very humane. Here is what he said, as recorded on page 4277 of Hansard for May 27, 1960: -never since confederation has it been possible for a postmaster general to record in one annual report, as I will today, such a wide range of new development and progress both internally and in service to the public.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I find that there is a rather important point lacking in the minister's statement. It is recognized that when he sat on the opposite side, the present Fostmaster General used to set himself up as the champion and defender of postal workers, and spent hours demanding fair treatment on their behalf. However, in his long speech of May 27, 1960, he did not see fit to refer even once to the position in which they find themselves today. I was particularly struck by one sentence in his speech, which is recorded on page 4277 of Hansard for the same date. I quote:
-various other matters, some of which I will deal with in my report and others which X will not 

never since confederation has it been possible
Mr. Chairman, I think the matters the minister did not even have time to mention are precisely those relating to the welfare of his departmental staff. The minister reviewed the great achievements of his department; its reorganization, the creation of a comptroller's branch, and on the matter of equipment, developments in stamp-vending machines, mailmobiles, delivery carts, plastic mailboxes and an increase in accounting post offices.
Those are strictly material matters, Mr. Chairman, and I ask the Postmaster General to give some thought to the human aspect of his department, because post office employees are in a sad plight and are clamouring for salary increases.
A very definite question was put to the minister the other day; I shall put it to him again. Fifty thousand civil servants have been or will be granted a salary increase this year by the federal government. I ask the minister to tell us how many post office employees, out of those 50,000 civil servants, have obtained a similar increase.
Every day, like many of my colleagues on this or the other side of the house, I receive

representations from post office employees, asking for the salary increase to which they are entitled.
It seems to me that the Postmaster General who, when he sat on this side of the house, used to feel sorry for the underpaid civil servants shows little inclination to devote as much time and energy defending the human beings employed in his department since his appointment as the minister of promises. He refers to machinery and electronic mail sorting or automatic segregator machines but he completely overlooks the salary increases which he had promised postal employees.
I find, for instance, that postal workers did not get a single increase since the Conservative party has been in power. The pay boost they received immediately after the present government's election had been recommended by the previous Liberal administration.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I declare without any hesitation-and the minister might note my words-that postal workers are the least paid employees in the whole civil service, in relation to their duties and the work they perform. Can the minister tell us why those employees get no attention from the present government despite their repeated representations? I have no intention at this time to remind the minister of all the requests made. He is more familiar with them than I am, and the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) covered the subject on May 27 last. I might, however, ask the minister to forget his machines for a moment. Otherwise, as pointed out earlier by the member for St. Denis, he is apt to become known as the "electronic minister". Let him think of the human beings employed by the government and particularly by the Post Office Department and come out and state whether or not the civil servants in his department can expect a raise and better treatment.
I know several postal workers who are forced to work on the sly at night, to earn a living and make both ends meet. The cost of living is steadily rising. Everything is higher, except the salaries of our civil servants, and if we had been able to examine the civil service commission report, we would surely have found in it recommendations of greater assistance to postal workers.
Would the minister therefore tell us in his remarks whether post office employees
Supply-Post Office
are justified in clamouring for salary increases-I think they are-and why their claims are unheeded when they ask the Post Office Department for a salary increase.
I should like the minister to note these remarks.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after an hour and three quarters spent in listening to these recriminations and complaints, I have to remind myself, and perhaps the committee at the same time, that as I suggested in my opening remarks we are now delivering more mail with fewer complaints than ever before in the history of the post office. In the past two years we have had more new developments and progress, both internally and in service to the public, than in any other similar period in our history. I think it is well that these two things should remain in the minds of the people in this chamber. There are few of us who are perfect, except perhaps the post office critic of the opposition. I was in that position when I sat over there. Now that I occupy this post I realize how fallible human beings and large organizations are. Possibly some of the criticisms which were made here this afternoon have been made year after year to minister after minister under government after government because it is impossible to take any tremendously large organization and make it, to use a phrase, letter perfect. However, the fact does remain that we are doing a better job now than ever before in our history.
I should like, if I could before six o'clock, to answer the points which have been raised, perhaps briefly. The hon. member for St. Denis, referring to my remarks in the United States and connecting them with the post office, said that the solution to this entire problem was to raise rates on United States printed material coming into Canada.
I did not say it should be, but it might be.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
He
forgets, of course, that this material is mailed in the United States where we have no control whatever over the rates and under the international postal agreement we are obliged to accept this matter at the Canadian border and deliver it.
He made a remark today about the electronic machine and the way it was chewing

Supply-Post Office
up the mail. I might point out to him that this is amusing because the electronic machine, as I pointed out in my earlier remarks, is not yet in operation. He speaks about Univac, which he says comes from England. It is evident he is getting his information from the wrong source. This machine is produced by the Remington Rand Company in the United States. The hon. member will be interested that it has absolutely nothing whatever to do with the processing of the mail. It is a calculating machine and computer and is used in connection with our post office savings bank and money order business.
In so far as the mailmobiles are concerned, I think it is quite safe to say, and draw the inference from my earlier remarks as well, that this has been a successful experiment and we will be continuing to enlarge the use of these vehicles. As I pointed out, at the moment we are comparing United States built vehicles and Canadian built vehicles. There is no final decision yet as to the type of vehicle that will be used. Unlike the hon. member for St. Denis, I am not one who wants to buy and use equipment in large quantities until I have found out that it is going to be the best equipment and the most satisfactory.
To turn to the hon. member for Port Arthur may I say this? I thank the hon. member for Port Arthur and other hon. members who have spoken for the thoughtful remarks they have made. The hon. member for Port Arthur referred primarily to the football pools and to a campaign of the last two years. Actually this has been a continuous process for a long period of time. The simple and full answer is that under sections 177 and 179 of the Criminal Code these sports pools and lotteries are illegal. It is a decision of parliament. I therefore have an obligation not to accept this illegal material for transmission in the mail. The course open to the hon. member for Port Arthur, if he wishes to change it, is merely to have parliament change the Criminal Code.
We will consider the situation so far as Sioux Lookout and Hornepayne are concerned with respect to the use of group boxes there.
He had an observation to make on our rural lists. We keep these lists as much up to date as possible and they are corrected periodically by the local postmaster. However, it is almost an impossibility with our

changing population to have these lists always correct.
He referred to the delivery of mail arriving in the city-that is the letter carrier delivered mail-after the letter carriers have left. May I say that we schedule our transportation facilities as much as possible to have mail arriving into cities in the morning and we adjust our letter carrier services to fit into this pattern. However there are always going to be locations and times when mail will arrive after the letter carrier has left. The easiest answer for business firms that require mail immediately, as many of them do, is to take post office boxes in the local post office. We will see what can be done about a marine post office at the lake-head.
As far as the hon. member for New Westminster is concerned, I appreciated his remarks and I know how much consideration he has given to this subject and what a problem it is to him. It is a problem to us as well. I would point out to him that this entire area has been offered in the last few months vastly improved mail service through the provision of letter carrier service, if my memory serves me rightly, to some 6,000 people or 7,000 people in that area. This is a tremendous improvement for these people over having to go to some local post office and pick up their mail themselves, as so many of them had to do in the past.
I believe he also knows that we are looking at the question of a post office building for that area. However, we do not want to be drawn into the erection of a building on a specific location in an area which is expanding and growing as rapidly as is that one until at least there is some firm indication as to the pattern of growth which is going to take place in the years ahead. I think we are borne out in this course by the very fact that their own local county council, or whatever the organization is which had planned the building for their governmental purposes, has delayed construction of the building at least for the present until they can see more clearly what the development is going to be.
The hon. member for Papineau asked me about a world refugee stamp. I am also sorry that we could not produce one. The time was a little bit too short for that purpose from the time when we were requested to do so and particularly the issue would have conflicted with two other stamps which were no more important, I admit, but for which we had committed ourselves a considerable time ago. I would point out, however, that

we are using widely across Canada in our cancelling machine cancellations in support of world refugee year.
I thank the hon. member for Waterloo North for his helpful observations and I will see what can be done about the matters he mentioned.
As far as the hon. member for Vancouver East is concerned, I answered as completely as I could the points that he raised when I was last on my feet on May 27. This is a question of opinion and I expressed my opinion, at that time.
As to the hon. member for St. John's East who spoke about revenue post offices in Newfoundland, may I say that we can have but one policy for buildings right across Canada. I think the weakness in the suggestion he put forward-and I say this without any criticism-was contained in his own observation that in these areas where they would like to have a government building constructed they cannot afford one for themselves and the postmaster cannot afford to put a special one up because his revenue is only a few hundred dollars a year. In these circumstances there is very little point in putting up a special government building. We depend upon local quarters provided by the postmaster. If there is any change in this principle it will apply just as well to Newfoundland as it will to all other parts of Canada.
The hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville inquired with regard to salaries of employees in the Post Office Department. He will perhaps recall that the Minister of Finance had indicated that this matter would be given very serious consideration. I am hopeful that an interesting announcement will be made in that respect when an opportunity for this consideration has been available to the bodies which must do so. As he knows, the present practice is to examine government employees group by group and to make recommendations. The first of these have been acted on and others are coming forward steadily.
